purpose: The Swallow lands between the Happy Prince's feet for the night, then looks up to find the gilded statue weeping tears from his sapphire eyes in the moonlight.

text.speaker: c_swallow

claim_map.how: p1 establishes the moonlit city and the statue on the tall column; p2 shows the Swallow alighting between the Prince's feet on the column top; p3 a single tear falls on him; p4 a second tear falls and he looks up at the Prince's sad face; p5 reveals the Prince's face filled with tears running down his golden cheeks, with the Swallow's off-panel 'Who are you?' asking the hook.

purpose: The Prince tells the Swallow why he weeps: he lived joyfully in Sans-Souci never knowing tears, but now sees the city's misery from on high and cannot help weeping despite his leaden heart.

panels.beat: The Prince on his column at night, the Swallow at his feet, speaking gently of his past life.

text.speaker: c_prince
text.text: When I was alive and had a human heart, I lived in Sans-Souci, where sorrow is not allowed to enter.

panels.beat: Memory of Sans-Souci: the joyful life within the walls.

text.text: In the garden he played. In the evening he led the dance.

panels.beat: The lofty wall — and beyond it, the city's misery he can now see from his high column.

text.text: They have set me here so high I can see all the misery of my city.

panels.beat: The Prince's sad face: a leaden heart that cannot choose but weep.

text.speaker: c_prince
text.text: Though my heart is made of lead yet I cannot chose but weep.

claim_map.how: p1: Prince says he lived in Sans-Souci where sorrow cannot enter (paraphrase). p2: flashback narration shows the joyful Sans-Souci life (garden, dance). p3: narration shows he has been set so high he can see the city's misery (paraphrase), visually the column rising above dark rooftops. p4: close of Prince's sad face with the leaden-heart line verbatim — 'I cannot chose but weep'.

purpose: At the warm mill, the Miller preaches that troubled friends should be left alone, his wife flatters him, and his youngest son is silenced for offering to share his porridge with Hans.

text.text: People in trouble should be left alone, and not be bothered by visitors.

panels.beat: The Wife, seated comfortably by the fire, praises her husband's fine thoughts.

text.speaker: c_miller_wife

purpose: The Miller trades his broken wheelbarrow for Hans's plank and a basket so full of primroses that Hans has none left for market.

purpose: The Miller sends Hans to market with a heavy sack of flour on a hot, dusty day; Hans returns exhausted but glad he did not refuse his best friend.

claim_map.how: p1 shows the Miller sending Hans on an errand with a heavy sack of flour to market; p2-3 show Hans carrying it on a hot, dusty road; p4-5 show him returning exhausted but loyal. This page dramatises the first of the Miller's many errands (flour to market); the other errands (mending the barn-roof, driving the sheep to the mountain) are introduced on the next pages of the section, so together the section conveys that the Miller constantly sends Hans on errands.

purpose: After reaching the Doctor's house, Hans loses his way in the worsening storm on the dangerous moor and is found drowned the next day in a great pool of water.

purpose: At Hans's funeral the Miller postures as chief mourner, then at the inn laments chiefly that he will not after all have to give away his wheelbarrow.

purpose: The Linnet shrugs off the Miller's fate after telling the story; the Water-rat furiously shouts 'Pooh!' at the moral and dives into his hole; the Duck arrives warning that moral-tales are dangerous.

text.speaker: c_water_rat
text.text: But what became of the Miller?

panels.beat: Linnet shrugs that he doesn't know or care — and remarks there is a moral.

text.speaker: c_linnet_s4
text.text: Oh! I don't know, and I don't care.

claim_map.how: p1 (big tall panel) shouts 'Pooh!' at the moral, with narration 'whisked with his tail into his hole' — the furious shout and the retirement into the hole. p2: Water-rat asks 'But what became of the Miller?' (the question that triggers the moral debate). p3: Linnet says he doesn't know or care and points out 'there's a moral, you see.' Together these cover: concludes story, knows/cares nothing about the Miller, angrily says moral and shouts Pooh, retires to his hole.

p4: the Duck arrives and directly warns 'Ah! that is always a very dangerous thing to do' — this IS the warning that telling a story with a moral is dangerous (the danger of which the narrator agrees).

purpose: Open 'The Remarkable Rocket': a Russian Princess arrives by swan-shaped sledge from Finland to marry the King's son, the Page wins a doubled (nonexistent) salary, and a grand display of fireworks is ordered for midnight in the royal garden.
